topic: LLM Inference: Quantize Weights, Not Your Sanity
postText:
Local medical LLM ate 40GB VRAM for one 7B model. One patient query. GPU node dead.

At the hospital where I work, we wanted on-prem LLM inference for clinical note summarization. PHI never leaves the building. Good plan. Bad first attempt.

Default FP16 weights for a 7B model = ~14GB. KV cache for 8K context across 4 concurrent requests = another ~20GB. Add CUDA overhead. OOM. The GPU node fell over on the first real shift.

What fixed it, in order of impact:

1. 4-bit weight quantization (GPTQ/AWQ). Weights dropped 14GB → ~4GB. Quality held for our summarization task. We validated on 200 anonymized notes before shipping.

2. Keep KV cache in FP16. Quantizing the KV cache too is tempting. Don't. Attention precision collapses on long clinical documents. We measured it. BLEU dropped, hallucinations rose.

3. PagedAttention + prefix caching. vLLM pages KV blocks like OS virtual memory, killing fragmentation. Our system prompt (long clinical instruction block) stays cached across requests. TTFT dropped ~40%.

4. Offload cold layers to CPU RAM. Layers not in the active batch stream back on demand. VRAM saved ~60%. Latency hit only on cold start.

Result: 4 concurrent clinical users, 8K context, one 24GB consumer GPU. No cloud. No PHI leak. No 2AM page.

The lesson: inference optimization is not one knob. It's a budget. Weights, KV cache, context length, concurrency — every gain on one side costs somewhere else. Measure on YOUR workload, not a benchmark blog.

Question for the engineers here: when you quantize for production, do you validate on a fixed eval set before shipping, or do you trust the community benchmark numbers? I've seen both go wrong.

If this saved you a GPU node, hit Like. Drop your quantization war stories in the comments. Share with your ML infra team before their next OOM.
